column3: The Hebrew refers to the father’s beds in the plural and leaves the defiling subject implicit; BSB uses singular bed and explicitly names Reuben.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls these Joel’s sons; BSB uses descendants.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew ends with he was a leader of the Reubenites; BSB repeats Beerah’s name.
The Hebrew calls the relatives his brothers; BSB uses relatives.
The Hebrew describes the settler with singular he; BSB uses plural they.
The Hebrew continues with singular he settled, where BSB uses they. It describes the entrance to the wilderness from the Euphrates, whereas BSB describes a desert extending to the river.
The Hebrew says the Hagrites fell into their hand and that they settled in their tents; BSB expresses defeat at their hands and occupation of the Hagrites’ homes.
The Hebrew says the sons of Gad lived opposite them; BSB uses descendants and explicitly identifies the Reubenites.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls these their brothers according to their fathers’ house; BSB uses kinsmen by families.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls Ahi head of their fathers’ house; BSB uses head of their family.
The Hebrew calls the associated towns daughters and adds their outer limits after Sharon’s pasturelands; BSB uses towns and leaves that final boundary phrase unstated.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew begins with their being helped and describes God as allowing Himself to be entreated; BSB puts their cry first and says He answered their prayers, repeating God’s name.
The Hebrew leaves the livestock owners unnamed and counts human souls; BSB names the Hagrites and describes the people as captives.
The Hebrew says they settled in their place; BSB says they occupied the land.
The Hebrew joins Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon with and; BSB identifies Senir and Mount Hermon as alternative names for Baal-hermon.
The Hebrew twice calls them heads of their fathers’ house and describes men of names; BSB uses heads of their families and famous men.
Close to the Hebrew.

The Hebrew repeats spirit for Pul and Tiglath-pileser and joins them with and; BSB identifies Tiglath-pileser parenthetically as Pul. It narrates the exile as a separate action, where BSB makes it the purpose of stirring the spirit.
